papers.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

papers.title: AI and the Two Margins of Work: Why Job Losses Show Up Before Job Creation
papers.abstract: Technological change acts on labor demand at two margins: adjustment within established activities and the creation of additional activities, often by new firms. Payroll statistics record the first promptly and the second late. In the computing era, firms that entered in 1978 or later held 42 percent of payroll by 1998 and entering cohorts kept about 80 percent of their payroll after five years; in the industries most exposed to automation, incumbents contracted before entrants accumulated, a sequence that is precise early in the period and suggestive by its end. We develop a model in which one AI capability lowers the full cost of acceptable output in existing production and makes additional projects worth attempting, with founder effort separate from hired hours. If operating products re-scale instantly, automation displaces no aggregate hours; if they take time, hours fall first and recover as incumbents re-expand and new products arrive, with the long-run sign set by income effects. Establishment job flows through the first quarter of 2026 show no gradient on language-model exposure on either margin, which is what the model predicts under the observed adoption path and also what no effect on payroll would look like; studies with founding-task exposure find entry rising 10 to 20 percent. We propose a net reinstatement ratio and show that statistics which record new work late overstate displacement for years.

papers.title: Menu Design Meets Market Design: Strategic Simplicity vs. Choice Complexity
papers.abstract: Strategic simplicity removes the incentive to misreport preferences, but it does not ensure that participants can identify what they prefer. We study this distinction in a laboratory experiment on serial dictatorships, where optimal play only requires choosing one's favorite bundle of real-effort tasks. Participants make fifteen incentivized choices among bundles that vary in how many tasks they combine. They choose either from a large menu or through a series of binary choices. Having made all choices, they unexpectedly reconsider each assignment against a previously rejected alternative. We find that roughly one in six choices is reversed and almost one in five involves an objectively dominated bundle. Simplifying the choice architecture does not help. Binary decomposition even raises reversal rates among low-ability participants and further inflates their confidence about their choices.

papers.title: Incomplete-market CAPM equilibria in continuous time
papers.abstract: We study continuous-time CAPM equilibria with general mean-variance preferences of the form $U(\mu,\sigma)$, where $U$ is strictly quasiconcave, increasing in the mean $\mu$ and decreasing in the volatility $\sigma$ of terminal wealth. Our framework accommodates both financial and productive assets with nontradeable endowments. We allow for equilibria driven by general semimartingales in the case of linear mean-variance preferences and by continuous semimartingales in the case of general mean-variance preferences. The key insight is a connection between mean-variance efficiency and quadratic utility maximisation. We first characterise quadratic equilibria through an explicit family of equilibrium price processes indexed by the aggregate risk tolerance. We then show that each agent's optimal mean-variance strategy corresponds to a quadratic optimum with an endogenously determined risk tolerance. This correspondence reduces the mean-variance equilibrium problem to a one-dimensional fixed-point problem, whose solvability we establish using fine properties of (dynamic) mean-variance hedging and a novel stability result for quadratic BSDEs with BMO growth at the origin. Finally, examples illustrate how unspanned stochastic-volatility risk interacts with aggregate endowments to affect equilibrium asset prices, and how nonlinear mean-variance preferences influence equilibrium risk tolerance and asset-price comparative statics.

papers.title: Match classification in the last round of four-team round-robin tournaments
papers.abstract: Classification of matches played in the last rounds of sports competitions is a well-established tool for evaluating tournament designs. Our paper offers the first comparison of deterministic and probabilistic match classification models by analysing the most prominent example of four-team round-robin competitions, the group stage of the FIFA World Cup. We show that both models are highly relevant in practice: all (four) deterministic and (six) probabilistic match types occurred in the 2014 and 2018 FIFA World Cups, respectively. The probabilistic model, which accounts for the relative benefits of attacking and defending, provides a deeper insight; for instance, the competitive matches from the deterministic approach can be of any of the six probabilistic types. Therefore, the probabilistic model is used to decompose the impact of three reforms introduced in the 2026 FIFA World Cup: the expansion to 48 teams, the modified qualification rules, and head-to-head tie-breakers.

papers.title: Social Media Can Suppress or Fuel Misinformation at Its Source, Depending on Civic Engagement
papers.abstract: Social media is widely viewed as a channel for spreading misinformation, but its effects may begin earlier, by shaping whether misinformation is produced in the first place. We examine whether social media suppresses or amplifies the supply of misinformation and identify civic engagement as a key boundary condition. Using data on the GDP reporting of Chinese local governments from 2011 to 2019, we find that social media adoption reduces GDP misreporting only when civic engagement is high. This reduction is driven by posts that disclose specific economic data rather than promotional content. When civic engagement is low, however, social media adoption instead increases GDP misreporting. These findings reveal a dual upstream role of social media in the misinformation process: it can deter misinformation at its source when disclosures are exposed to engaged citizens, but can amplify its supply when civic engagement is limited.

papers.title: Tolerable Inflation, Intolerable Uncertainty
papers.abstract: How much of an inflation deviation a central bank should tolerate is a well-defined optimum in the New Keynesian model, but it cannot be identified: optimal accommodation of supply shocks and an unwarranted drift of the effective inflation target are observationally equivalent. This impossibility has a cost. A public that cannot verify the bank's intention prices each expected point of overshoot, so uncertainty about inflation is flat below the announced target and rises linearly above it: the observational-equivalence effect. Professional forecasts, swap and option markets and realized inflation all show this pattern, with the kink at the announced number. A second and larger effect produces the same shape: inflation is more volatile when it is high, and in realized inflation that level effect is mostly energy. Both effects load on the distance from the target, so the data admit the observational-equivalence effect without isolating it, and its cost cannot be estimated with the data at hand. We therefore cannot say how optimal monetary policy should change on its account, but three policy conclusions survive: in the textbook model, not observing the slope of the Phillips curve and the composition of shocks never calls for tolerating less; the announced target remains worth having, because it compresses beliefs at the target; and the central bank can monitor the point-years inflation spends above target, on which the effect is charged, and read inflation uncertainty net of the distance from the target. Normalized Uncertainty provides that reading. In French loan-level data, raw inflation uncertainty is unrelated to corporate loan rates after controls, whereas a one-standard-deviation increase in Normalized Uncertainty is associated with rates 89 basis points higher. The correction also reveals a negative association with growth across countries and alters euro-area time-series results.

papers.title: Social Networks and the Propagation of Household Shocks to Asset Prices
papers.abstract: When can local household disturbances move credit prices? I develop a financially weighted propagation operator on the social network. In a conditional household-intermediary equilibrium, its projection determines the household-demand component of the excess bond premium. Because responses decay at different rates across network patterns and channels, a location's relative financial importance generically changes with the horizon, so no single centrality measure summarizes exposure across horizons. Household measurements recover this projection exactly when they span independently measured demand sensitivities. Empirically, social exposure to storm-damaged counties is negatively associated with spending weeks later in counties outside the recorded footprints. In simulations on the observed network under the model's diffusion law, the operator predicts the propagated credit-premium component of held-out storms with about 30 percent less error than direct social exposure.

papers.title: Huge If True: Learning from the Size of the Surprise
papers.abstract: Responses to earnings surprises depend on an unknown multiplier mapping earnings to value. Investors, however, learn about the news and the multiplier from the same number. Large surprises may indicate small multipliers and tiny surprises large ones. We model how greater uncertainty about the multiplier attenuates responses on average but makes them steeper near zero surprises. In an incentivized experiment, we find that greater processing constraints lower average sensitivity but raise it near zero. We confirm this with real-world earnings announcements: stocks with higher valuation uncertainty, our proxy for multiplier uncertainty, respond less on average but more steeply near zero.
